extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and USPTO examiners (practitioners handling after-final practice, 37 CFR 1.116 replies, and petitions under 37 CFR 1.181)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment and procedures for (1) petitioning the Director under 37 CFR 1.181 to withdraw the finality of an Office action and (2) admission of rebuttal evidence filed under 37 CFR 1.116 after a final action. Covers when a final action is improper (new ground of rejection) and standards for admitting after-final amendments/evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 132(a) — notice and reexamination requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever, on examination, any claim for a patent is rejected, or any objection or requirement made, the Director shall notify the applicant thereof, stating the reasons for such rejection, or objection or requirement ... and if after receiving such notice, the applicant persists in his claim for a patent, with or without amendment, the application shall be reexamined. No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must give reasons for rejections/objections and reexamine if applicant persists; applicants must not introduce new matter in amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.113(a) — second-or-subsequent action can be final
rubrics_metrics.description: On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final, whereupon applicant's reply is limited to appeal or to amendment as specified in § 1.114 or § 1.116.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finality is ordinarily permitted on second/subsequent actions; applicant's options after finality are constrained to the statutory/regulated procedures (appeal or limited amendment).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.113(b) — examiner must state all grounds and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final action must identify and explain each ground of rejection so applicant understands the basis for the final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.113(c) — reply requirements to a final action
rubrics_metrics.description: Reply to a final rejection or action must include cancellation of, or appeal from the rejection of, each rejected claim. If any claim stands allowed, the reply must comply with any requirements or objections as to form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply to a final action cannot simply reargue — it must either cancel or appeal each rejected claim (or present authorized amendments); if a claim is allowed, formal requirements must be met.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.116(b)(3) and (a) — amendments touching the merits after final
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment touching the merits of the application may be admitted after a final rejection or action upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the amendment is necessary and was not earlier presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After-final substantive amendments are exceptional and require a showing of good and sufficient reasons for both necessity and why the amendment was not earlier presented; otherwise only certain limited amendments (e.g., canceling claims) are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.116(e) — admission of affidavits or other evidence after final
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or other evidence submitted after a final rejection or other final action ... but before or on the same date of filing an appeal may be admitted upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the affidavit or other evidence is necessary and was not earlier presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is critical: evidence filed after final can be entered only if filed before or on the same date as an appeal notice and only with a showing of good and sufficient reasons. Evidence that is non-public (e.g., 1.132 declarations) has different character than publicly available literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP § 706.07(a) — limitation on introducing new grounds in subsequent final action
rubrics_metrics.description: Second or any subsequent actions on the merits shall be final, except where the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither necessitated by applicant's amendment of the claims, nor based on information submitted in an IDS filed during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner generally may not introduce a new ground of rejection in a final action unless it was necessitated by a claim amendment or arises from an IDS timely filed with required fee; use of IDS-submitted info may allow finality but introduction of other new grounds is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP § 706.x / practice — examiner may elaborate but not change basic thrust
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no new ground of rejection if the basic thrust of the rejection has remained the same such that the applicant has been given an opportunity to react; further explaining and elaboration upon a rejection are not considered a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in wording or added explanation that do not change the fundamental rationale or factual basis do not create a new ground; examiners are expected to respond to applicant arguments and may clarify or elaborate the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP § 1207.03(III) — 'basic thrust of the rejection' test for new grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A position or rationale that changes the 'basic thrust of the rejection' will give rise to a new ground of rejection. The examiner need not use identical language; different wording or restatement is permissible so long as the basic thrust is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the applicant had a fair opportunity to respond to the central rationale; if the rationale or facts relied on are new (new facts, new rationale, or new prior art not previously raised), it may be a new ground requiring withdrawal of finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: New ground of rejection indicators (case-law principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new ground of rejection may be present when a rejection relies upon new facts or a new rationale not previously raised to the applicant; mere different language or additional explanation addressing applicant's arguments is not a new ground (citing In re Biedermann, In re Leithem, In re Jung, In re Kronig, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to whether the final action relied on new data/rationale (e.g., newly cited experimental data, curves, tables, or articles not previously on record) that were not necessitated by amendment or timely IDS; if so, applicant may be unfairly surprised and finality may be improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a final action need not be withdrawn despite added supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: If the basic thrust remains the same and added materials (e.g., graphs, tables, articles) are responsive elaboration or are used to explain the previously-stated rejection, then the finality need not be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from decision: reproduction of the same data point from a reference already cited in non-final action and use of articles as exemplars of peer-reviewed research supporting the same rationale do not necessarily create a new ground; examiner can elaborate to respond to applicant's arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and sufficient reasons standard for entry of rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence submitted after a final action may be entered if the applicant shows 'good and sufficient reasons' why the evidence is necessary and was not earlier presented (37 CFR 1.116(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treated a collection of publicly-available technical publications filed in response to new points raised in a final action as meeting the 'good and sufficient reasons' test because the materials were directly responsive to the final action's content and did not present non-public facts under 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedural limits for post-final submissions (inter partes/ex parte distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding general provisions, certain types of after-final amendments or evidence are prohibited in inter partes reexamination after appeal notice except as provided in specified sections; similar restrictions apply in ex parte reexamination contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to the specific proceeding type (ex parte vs inter partes reexamination) and the cited CFR/MPEP sections that impose narrower limits on after-final actions or evidence (e.g., 1.116(d)(1)/(2), §1.981, §41.77(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner expectations regarding foreseeability of applicant amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner cannot be expected to foresee whether or how an applicant will amend a claim to overcome a rejection except in very limited circumstances (e.g., where examiner suggests how applicant can overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The permissibility of making an action final when new prior art is cited depends in part on whether the new rejection was reasonably foreseeable from earlier prosecution; absence of foreseeability may counsel against finality when new grounds are introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequence / appellate timing after petition decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If a petition decision denies withdrawal of finality but grants entry of evidence, the application proceeds and an appeal timeline applies (e.g., two months from decision mailing to file an appeal brief under 37 CFR 41.37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should note appellate deadlines and extension rules (37 CFR 1.136, MPEP §1205.01) after a petition decision and plan filings accordingly.
